``` ============================================================================ Quadratic GIF comment concatenation allows DoS in Image.open() Location: src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:266 in GifImageFile._seek() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` Opening a crafted GIF file with `Image.open()` takes time that grows with the square of the file's size, so anyone who can submit an image to a service that uses Pillow can keep one worker busy at full processor load for a long time with a small file. A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside `Image.open()` itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py`, which builds `info["comment"]` by appending to an immutable `bytes` object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (`comment += block`, line 261) and once per comment extension (`info["comment"] += b" " + comment`, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)`, any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB). This is the same kind of issue as the EPS open-phase slowdown fixed as CVE-2021-28677, here in the GIF comment handling. The quadratic pattern was introduced in commit b2b737b68b06 ("Allow arbitrary number of comment extension subblocks", November 2018) and has shipped since Pillow 5.4.0. The attached script builds 2 MB and 4 MB test files and compares each against a byte-identical control whose extensions are labelled as plain text instead of comment. The 4 MB comment file took about 34 seconds to open, against 0.26 seconds for its control. A patch that collects the pieces in a list and joins them once is also attached. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` collects GIF comment extensions into `info["comment"]` using `bytes` concatenation, once per 255-byte sub-block and once per comment extension, with no limit on the total. `bytes` is immutable, so every `+=` allocates a new object and copies everything accumulated so far; the work done by `Image.open()` is therefore quadratic in the amount of comment data in frame 0. A 1×1 GIF89a whose body is nothing but the 5-byte comment extension `21 FE 01 41 00` repeated makes this directly observable. `Image.open(BytesIO(data))` on such a file, stock build at this commit, 2-CPU machine: | file size | comment extensions (`21 FE …`) | same bytes labelled plain-text extension (`21 01 …`) | |---|---|---| | 1 MB | 1.2 s | 0.09 s | | 2 MB | 4.9 s | 0.13 s | | 4 MB | 35 s | 0.26 s | | 8 MB | 183 s | — | The control column is the identical byte stream with the extension label changed from `0xFE` to `0x01`; it goes through the same loop and the same `self.data()` reads but is discarded instead of concatenated, and scales linearly. No `load()` is needed and no warning or exception is raised; `im.info["comment"]` simply ends up holding the multi-megabyte blob. The code, `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py:229-281` (trimmed): ```python elif s == b"!": s = self.fp.read(1) block = self.data() … elif s[0] == 254: # # comment extension # comment = b"" # Read this comment block while block: comment += block # :261 one copy per sub-block block = self.data() if "comment" in info: # If multiple comment blocks in frame, separate with info["comment"] += b" " + comment # :266 one copy per extension else: info["comment"] = comment s = b"" continue … while self.data(): # every other extension: read and drop pass ``` `self.data()` (`:97-102`) reads one length byte and then that many bytes, so each call is cheap and bounded; the cost is entirely in the two `+=` lines. For a single comment extension of N bytes delivered as N/255 sub-blocks, line 261 copies about N²/510 bytes in total (4 MB → 2.3 s, 8 MB → 9.5 s, 16 MB → 38 s measured). Splitting the same data into many small comment extensions is worse, because line 266 re-copies the whole of `info["comment"]` once per extension: with 1-byte extensions a file of F bytes causes roughly F²/25 bytes of copying, which is the table above (growth ×4–7 per doubling once the buffer outgrows the CPU caches). The simplest case is a `/Pages` root that lists itself as its own `/Parent`; a longer cycle among page-tree nodes behaves the same way. The loop performs no I/O and no allocation, so neither `MemoryError` nor the recursion limit intervenes. A longer cycle behaves identically as long as every node on it was reached through `linearize_page_tree()` and is therefore cached (e.g. root 2 → `/Kids [4 0 R]`, node 4 → `/Kids [3 0 R] /Parent 2 0 R`, and root 2 declaring `/Parent 4 0 R`); a `/Parent` pointing at an object that was never read raises `KeyError` instead, which is harmless. The parser already defends against exactly this shape of problem one level up: `read_prev_trailer()` (`src/PIL/PdfParser.py:699-722`) carries a `processed_offsets` list and raises `PdfFormatError("trailer loop found")` when a `/Prev` offset repeats — the fix for CVE-2026-42310. The `/Parent` walk in `rewrite_pages()` has no equivalent guard. The unguarded walk was introduced in `24ecfe315ab5` ("issue #2959: fix wrong Parent of pre-existing Page objects when appending", 2018-03-03) and has been in every release since 5.1.0. ## Impact Any application that appends pages to a PDF it did not produce — `im.save(fp, "PDF", append=True)` or `save_all=True, append=True` on a user-supplied document — hangs indefinitely with one CPU core pinned, on an input of a few hundred bytes. The loop is pure Python doing two dict lookups per iteration, so memory stays flat and memory limits do not end it; only an external watchdog does. In a web worker or batch converter that is a denial of service of that worker per request. The attacker needs to control only the bytes of the existing PDF; no non-default Pillow setting is involved beyond the application choosing the append path. Pillow does not open PDFs for reading, so plain `Image.open()` pipelines are not affected. This is a sibling of CVE-2026-42310 (infinite loop on a cyclic trailer `/Prev` chain in the same parser, same entry point): same class, different linked structure, and the guard added for that CVE does not cover it. ## Reproducing `repro` is a single Python script that runs against the installed Pillow (`/src/src/PIL`). Each has a Catalog (object 1), a `/Pages` root (object 2) and a `/Page` (object 3), and each has a correct xref table. The only difference between them is in object 2: - `control` has `<>`. ``` ============================================================================ APNG background disposal allocates full canvas before decompression bomb check Location: src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:1000  in PngImageFile._seek() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A 126-byte animated PNG file makes Pillow's `Image.open()` allocate and fill memory sized by the image dimensions the file claims, before Pillow's built-in check for oversized images runs. A file claiming 22000×22000 pixels costs about 1.9 GB. Anyone who can get an application to open an image they supply, with default settings and no further calls such as `load()`, can cause a multi-gigabyte memory spike per file. If the claimed size exceeds the machine's free memory, the operating system kills the process outright.  The bug is in `PngImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py` (around line 1000). For any APNG, `_open()` calls `self._seek(0)`. When the first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `_seek()` calls `Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)` with the full IHDR size, which allocates and zero-fills width×height×4 bytes. `OP_PREVIOUS` takes the same path, because frame 0 rewrites it to `OP_BACKGROUND`. This all happens inside the plugin factory, so `Image.open()`'s `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)` only runs after the memory has been touched. A 1×1 frame rectangle passes the only checks on the way.  Below available memory, the allocation is freed when `DecompressionBombError` propagates, so sustained pressure needs repeated or concurrent uploads. A 45000×45000 header gets the process killed by the out-of-memory killer on an 8 GB host. The attached reproducer opens two such files that differ in one byte (`dispose_op` 0 vs 1). Both end in `DecompressionBombError`, but peak resident memory is 17 MB for the first and 1864 MB for the second. The eager fill was introduced in 5e4e0fa6ee67 ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", December 2020) and first shipped in 8.1.0. Two candidate patches with a regression test are attached.  ## Details  For an APNG whose first `fcTL` chunk requests `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal, `PngImageFile._open()` creates and zero-fills a core image of the full IHDR-declared size. This happens inside the plugin factory, i.e. before `Image.open()` gets to `_decompression_bomb_check(im.size)`, so the check that is meant to reject oversized headers without allocating anything runs only after the allocation has been made and touched.  The following 126-byte file (all chunk lengths and CRCs valid) makes `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))`, with default `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` and no `load()`, reach 1.86 GB resident (`ru_maxrss`) and then raise `DecompressionBombError`. The byte-identical file with `dispose_op=0` raises the same error at 17 MB.  ``` IHDR  width=22000 height=22000 bit_depth=8 colour_type=6 (RGBA) acTL  num_frames=2 num_plays=0 fcTL  seq=0 w=1 h=1 x=0 y=0 delay=1/10 dispose_op=1 (OP_BACKGROUND) blend_op=0 IDAT  zlib(00 00 00 00 00)                      # one 1x1 RGBA scanline IEND ```  With `width=height=45000` (8.1 GB canvas) the same call attempts the full allocation: under a 4 GiB `RLIMIT_AS` it fails with `MemoryError` from the allocator instead of `DecompressionBombError`; without a cap, on an 8 GB host with no swap, the process is OOM-killed.  ### Code path  `Image.open()` runs the bomb check only after the plugin's constructor (and therefore `_open()`) has returned:  ```python # src/PIL/Image.py:3699-3701                     im = factory(fp, filename)                     _decompression_bomb_check(im.size)                     return im ```  For a plain PNG that ordering is fine: `PngImageFile._open()` only parses chunks up to the first `IDAT` and records `self._size` from `IHDR`; nothing is allocated from it. For an APNG (`acTL` seen, so `im_n_frames` is set) `_open()` additionally positions on frame 0:  ```python # src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:845-853         if self.png.im_n_frames is not None:             …             self._seek(0) ```  `_seek(0)` copies `disposal` and `bbox` from the `fcTL` chunk into `self.dispose_op` / `self.dispose_extent` and then prepares the disposal image for the *next* frame eagerly, using the full image size:  ```python # src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:991-1001         if self._prev_im is None and self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:             self.dispose_op = Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND          self.dispose = None         if self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_PREVIOUS:             …         elif self.dispose_op == Disposal.OP_BACKGROUND:             self.dispose = Image.core.fill(self.mode, self.size)             self.dispose = self._crop(self.dispose, self.dispose_extent) ```  `Image.core.fill` is `_fill()` in `src/_imaging.c:711`, which does `ImagingNewDirty(mode, xsize, ysize)` followed by `ImagingFill()`; `ImagingFill` (`src/libImaging/Fill.c:23`) writes every row, so the whole `width*height*4` bytes become resident rather than merely reserved. `self.size` here is the IHDR size (22000×22000), not the 1×1 frame rectangle. The `_crop` on the next line does call `_decompression_bomb_check`, but on the `fcTL` rectangle (1×1) and only after the fill has completed. Lines 991-992 rewrite `OP_PREVIOUS` to `OP_BACKGROUND` on frame 0, so `dispose_op=2` takes the same path (verified: identical 1.86 GB peak). When the first `fcTL` rectangle is large, the `_crop` copy is a second extent-sized buffer on top of the full-canvas fill, so the transient peak can reach about twice the canvas: a 13000×13000 full-frame `fcTL` (below the error threshold, so `Image.open()` succeeds with only a `DecompressionBombWarning`) peaks at 1.31 GB for a 0.66 GB canvas.  The only validation `chunk_fcTL` applies (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:740-745`) is that the frame rectangle fits inside the IHDR size, which a 1×1 frame always does; IHDR width/height themselves are unconstrained 32-bit values at this point. Control then returns to `_open_core`, `_decompression_bomb_check((22000, 22000))` raises, and the 1.9 GB core image is released when the half-constructed `PngImageFile` is discarded.  The eager full-size fill in `_seek()` was introduced in `5e4e0fa6ee67` ("Use disposal settings from previous frame", 2020-12-24) and first shipped in 8.1.0; before it, the `OP_BACKGROUND` fill lived in `load_end()` and could not be reached from `Image.open()`.  ## Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` on untrusted bytes with default settings — the configuration in which the decompression-bomb check is supposed to make that call cheap and safe — can be made to allocate and write an attacker-chosen amount of memory from a ~126-byte PNG upload, before any error is reported and without `load()`, frame iteration, or `LOAD_TRUNCATED_IMAGES`. The amount is set directly by the IHDR width/height (4 bytes per pixel for colour type 6): values below the host's free memory cause a transient multi-GB spike per request (≈15,000,000× amplification at 22000×22000) that is freed when the exception propagates, so concurrent or repeated uploads are needed to sustain pressure; values above it get the worker process OOM-killed outright. PNG is accepted by essentially every upload pipeline, and the file passes `_accept` and chunk CRC checks as a well-formed APNG.  This is the same class as the recent bomb-check additions for WMF (load at a different DPI), FITS, GIF and FontFile — an allocation sized from file-declared numbers on a path `_decompression_bomb_check` does not cover — but here the uncovered path is `Image.open()` itself rather than a later `load()`/`seek()`.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script (no build step, no companion files). It builds two PNGs in memory, opens each one with plain `Image.open(io.BytesIO(data))` in a fresh child interpreter using default settings and no `load()`, and has each child report the exception it got and its own peak RSS (`ru_maxrss`). It needs about 2 GB of free RAM and finishes in about a second.  The two files are 126 bytes each and differ in exactly one byte, the `dispose_op` of the first `fcTL` chunk: `0` (`OP_NONE`) for the control and `1` (`OP_BACKGROUND`) for the attack. Both declare IHDR 22000×22000 RGBA. That is 484 Mpixel, above the 2×`MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` error threshold, so `Image.open()` has to reject both with `DecompressionBombError`. Each chunk has a job:  - The `acTL` chunk (2 frames) makes `_open()` call `_seek(0)`. - The 1×1 `fcTL` rectangle passes `chunk_fcTL`'s bounds check and `_crop`'s bomb check. - The one-scanline `IDAT` ends header parsing.  Expected output on this tree:  ``` 126-byte APNG declaring 22000x22000 RGBA; Image.open(BytesIO(data)), defaults   control  dispose_op=0 OP_NONE        -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS    17 MB   attack   dispose_op=1 OP_BACKGROUND  -> DecompressionBombError peak RSS  1864 MB Image.open() touched a full 22000x22000 canvas before the bomb check ran BUG ```  Both files are rejected, but the control is rejected at interpreter size. The attack file only reaches the bomb check after `Image.core.fill("RGBA", (22000, 22000))` has allocated and zero-filled about 1.9 GB. The script prints `BUG` if the attack child's peak RSS is at least 1000 MB and at least 20× the control's, or if the attack child is killed by `SIGKILL` (for example by the OOM killer on a small host). Otherwise it prints `OK`; any other non-zero child exit is treated as a harness failure, printed with the child's output, and also ends in `OK`. With either attached patch applied, both children report about 17–22 MB and the script prints `OK`.  The allocation grows with the header, so it can be scaled by changing `SIZE` in the script. The 45000×45000 case (an 8.1 GB canvas) is covered in Details and is not part of the script.  ## Suggested fix  Do not build the `OP_BACKGROUND` disposal image from the declared size during `_open()`. ### Summary The MSP RLE decoder expands run-length data into an in-memory buffer with no cap tied to the declared image size. A small file that passes the pixel-count check can force hundreds of megabytes or more of allocation when the application loads pixels.  ### Details The MSP decoder writes each run into an unbounded `io.BytesIO` and can expand roughly 85x per run:  - `src/PIL/MspImagePlugin.py:144-146`  ### Impact Memory-exhaustion denial of service from a tiny crafted image in any application that loads pixels. The expansion is decoupled from the declared pixel count, so `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` does not bound it.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:94  in _tiffWriteProc() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  Pillow can write attacker-chosen data past the end of a heap buffer when it saves a TIFF image to an in-memory destination such as `io.BytesIO` rather than to a file. The same code also copies leftover heap memory from the process into the saved file. Anyone who can supply an image to a service that opens it and re-saves it as TIFF this way can trigger this with default settings. The attached reproducer crashes the process, and the overflow could potentially be developed further, but code execution is not demonstrated here.  The bug is in `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. This is the write callback for the in-memory sink that Pillow gives libtiff whenever the save target has no `fileno()`. While writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the current end of data and writes tag values there. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of from the write position `state->loc`. As a result, the first out-of-line tag value written after that seek can run past the allocation by up to the size of the directory: 12 bytes per entry, 126 bytes in the minimal case, and 2384 bytes observed with a 331-entry directory. The overflowing bytes are the tail of a tag value taken from the uploaded file.  No save options are needed, because compression and tags are inherited from the source image. The overflow does require an attacker-sized out-of-line tag to reach libtiff. That happens when the opened TIFF is saved directly (ImageDescription, DocumentName or XMP), or through an embedded ICC profile, which survives `copy()` in `im.info`. The bytes libtiff skips for alignment are never initialised, so any compressed TIFF over 64 KiB written this way also leaks one stale heap byte per padding hole. That leak needs no crafted tag.  The attached reproducer builds a 131 KB PackBits TIFF and runs `Image.open(...).save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")`. Saving the same image to a file path succeeds, but the `BytesIO` save aborts with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. A second part of the script shows uninitialised heap bytes at the padding offsets of a `BytesIO` save that are zero in the file save. Saves to real files are unaffected. The defect dates to e782fe721e01 (2013) and has been present since Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Details  When `im.save()` writes a TIFF through libtiff to a target that has no usable `fileno()` (`io.BytesIO`, an HTTP response object, a storage backend stream), libtiff is opened with `TIFFClientOpen()` on Pillow's own in-memory sink, `_tiffWriteProc` / `_tiffSeekProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c`. libtiff treats that sink like a file: when it writes the directory it seeks *beyond* the current end of data (to `eof + IFD size`, where the out-of-line tag values go, and one byte further after every odd-length tag value to keep offsets even) and writes there. On a real file the kernel grows the file and zero-fills the gap. The memory sink does neither correctly:  1. `_tiffWriteProc` sizes its `realloc()` from `state->size + size` instead of `state->loc + size`, so the first write after such a seek can land past the end of the new allocation — a heap buffer overflow whose content is tag data taken from the image being saved. 2. The bytes that libtiff skips are never written, and the grown region is a bare `realloc()`, so they reach the output TIFF with whatever the heap held before.  Both are reachable with default settings by the ordinary "re-encode the upload" sequence `Image.open(upload); im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with no save options: `compression` defaults to the source file's (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1734`), any compression other than raw selects the libtiff writer (`:1746`), the source's `tag_v2` entries are passed through to libtiff (`:1959`), and a target without `fileno()` leaves `_fp = 0` (`:1928-1935`), i.e. the memory sink. The overflow half additionally needs an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value of the right length to reach libtiff. With the opened `TiffImageFile` saved directly (`tag_v2` passthrough) that can be a ~64 KiB ASCII tag (269/270/271/272) or the XMP packet (tag 700, type BYTE — arbitrary bytes), and the number of tags the upload carries sets the IFD size, i.e. the overrun length (12 bytes per entry; 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD observed). After `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` the `tag_v2` entries are gone, but `im.info["compression"]` (still selecting libtiff) and `im.info["icc_profile"]` survive and the ICC profile is written as tag 34675 (`:1822-1824`), an equally attacker-controlled out-of-line value: `Image.open(x).copy().save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` with the payload in the ICC profile produces the identical ASan report. The stale-byte half needs no attacker tag at all.  **Proof (overflow).** A 131 198-byte hand-built TIFF — mode L, 7×8191, `Compression=32773` (PackBits), an `ImageDescription` of 65 535 characters — opened with `Image.open()` and saved with `im.save(io.BytesIO(), "TIFF")` aborts a stock build with glibc's `malloc(): corrupted top size`. The same call against an AddressSanitizer build of the C extensions reports  ``` AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... WRITE of size 65536  #1 _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:115  #4 TIFFFlush  #5 ImagingLibTiffEncode src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056 0 bytes to the right of 131072-byte region, allocated by realloc in _tiffWriteProc src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:103 ```  **Proof (uninitialised bytes).** Saving one 300×300 RGB image as `compression="tiff_lzw"` with four odd-length ASCII tags to a `BytesIO`, once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=1` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0xfe) and once with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (0x55), gives two 369 463-byte TIFFs that differ in exactly 4 bytes, 0xfe vs 0x55, at offsets 369177, 369417, 369423, 369451 — the pad byte between the odd-length last strip and the IFD, and the pad byte after each odd-length tag value except the last. Without any allocator tweaks, after a few 64 KB–400 KB Python `bytes` objects filled with 0xa7 are created and freed, re-saving an uploaded LZW TIFF carrying ten odd-length ASCII tags yields 0xa7 at all nine pad offsets.  ### Code walk-through  The sink's state is `{data, size (allocated), loc (position), eof (high-water mark)}`; the encoder path starts it as a zeroed 64 KiB block (`TiffDecode.c:863`, `calloc(bufsize, 1)` with `bufsize = 64*1024`, `flrealloc = 1`). The general condition is: at directory-write time the strip data ends within *IFD-size* bytes of the current allocation boundary, and the first out-of-line tag value has a length just below a multiple of 64 KiB. The overrun length is `IFD size + pad − slack`, so it grows by 12 bytes per additional tag. For single-band images (L, P, 1, I;16, F…) `BitsPerSample` is stored inline and the first out-of-line value in tag order is `DocumentName` (269) or `ImageDescription` (270) — both free-length ASCII strings taken from the source file. Pillow re-encodes the pixels itself, but with PackBits the compressed size is a deterministic function of attacker-chosen pixel rows (the reproducer uses rows of 7 distinct bytes → 8 bytes per row → exactly 65536 bytes including the 8-byte header), so the attacker controls both quantities. For multi-band images the 6-byte `BitsPerSample` array is written first and absorbs the growth, which is why RGB sources do not hit the overflow.  The disclosure half is the benign version of the same sequence. In the LZW/RGB trace the strip data ends at the odd offset 369177; libtiff places the IFD at 369178 and the tag values from 369364 on, and after each odd-length value seeks one byte forward before the next write (`seek off=369418 (loc=369417)`, `write size=5 at loc=369418`, …). Offsets 369177, 369417, 369423 and 369451 are therefore never written. They lie in the part of the buffer obtained by the `realloc()` calls at `:103` (the block grew 65536 → 196608 → 327680 → 458752 during the strip writes), which is not cleared, so the emitted file carries the previous heap contents at those positions. Holes that fall inside the initial 64 KiB are zero only because that block is `calloc`'d.  The defect was introduced in e782fe721e01 ("initial merge of wiredfool/Python-Imaging-Library-G4-Tiff-Support", 2013-03-08), first released in Pillow 2.0.0.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts an image and produces a TIFF rendition into a non-file object — the usual pattern for returning or uploading the result without touching disk — is exposed to whoever supplies the image, with no non-default Pillow setting involved. The overflow additionally requires that an attacker-controlled out-of-line tag value reaches libtiff: the uploaded ImageDescription/DocumentName/XMP when the application saves the opened TIFF itself (or copies its tags into the save), or the embedded ICC profile, which survives `convert()`/`resize()`/`thumbnail()`/`copy()` in `im.info` together with the compression. Under those conditions, with a crafted single-band TIFF the uploader gets a heap out-of-bounds write in the worker process of IFD-size bytes (12 bytes per directory entry the upload carries — 126 bytes with the minimal reproducer, 2384 bytes with a 331-entry IFD) immediately past a 128 KiB-class `realloc` block, with the overwritten bytes being the tail of a tag value they chose; on the stock build the minimal reproducer is detected by glibc and kills the process (`SIGABRT`).  Given two addresses leaked by a separate bug, this write has been turned into code execution against a stock build of this commit with ASLR/PIE/NX enabled and default settings (that proof-of-concept is not included with this report): a single-process stdlib `http.server` worker doing nothing but `Image.open(BytesIO(body)).save(BytesIO(), "TIFF")` per upload executed an attacker-chosen shell command (`id>/tmp/r.XXXXXX`), answered `200` and kept serving (12/12 against a freshly started worker, 2/6 after twenty unrelated uploads; a miss normally leaves the worker running and is retryable). The two addresses (`&system`, `&PyBytes_Type`) were taken from an unrelated information disclosure in the same process; everything else is this bug plus properties of Pillow's TIFF reader used as a heap-shaping script. The 4.7 MB attack TIFF is a 397×165 8-bit PackBits image whose rows re-encode to exactly 65 528 bytes (strip ends at sink offset 65 536), a 63 942-byte XMP packet (tag 700) as the first out-of-line value, and ~500 private IFD entries. Because `TiffImagePlugin` turns every IFD entry into one `bytes` object in IFD order, frees an earlier entry when a later one repeats its tag number, and parses the IFD three times per request (`TiffImagePlugin.py:1258`, `:1271`, and `getexif()` from `load_end()` at `:1331`), those entries drain glibc's free lists, punch exact-size holes for every large allocation the save makes, and arrange that the 128 KiB `realloc` of the sink lands directly below a live 0x540 chunk followed by libtiff's own `TIFF` handle (`malloc(1313)` from `TIFFClientOpen`). The 2384 overflowing bytes rewrite the start of the `TIFF` struct with the command string, a zeroed `tif_dir`, `tif_diroff = 65536`, and `tif_cleanup = system` at +0x3f8; libtiff resumes `TIFFWriteDirectorySec` on the modified handle and calls `(*tif->tif_cleanup)(tif)`. With gdb on `__libc_system` the call arrives as `__libc_system("id>/tmp/r.…") ← libtiff.so.6 ← TIFFFlush ← ImagingLibTiffEncode (src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1056) ← _encode (src/encode.c:139)`. Offsets are per-binary constants (glibc 2.36, CPython 3.12.14, libtiff 4.5.0, this `_imaging.so`), all obtainable from public distribution files.  Independently, every compressed TIFF written to such a target that exceeds 64 KiB discloses one byte of stale heap per alignment hole (one per odd-length tag value plus possibly one before the IFD; the count is set by the tags in the uploaded file) at predictable offsets in the returned file — low bandwidth, but it is other requests' freed data. File-path and real-fd targets (`TIFFFdOpen`) are unaffected by either issue. The primitive is the same class and attacker position as the `TiffDecode.c` decode-side heap overflows CVE-2020-35654, CVE-2021-25289 and CVE-2020-10379, but on the encode path and behind the output-to-a-non-file and tag-passthrough preconditions above, with code execution additionally depending on an address leak from another bug.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script that uses the installed Pillow, writes its inputs into a temporary directory. It has two parts. Each part compares saving to a file path, which goes through `TIFFFdOpen` and is correct, with the same save into an `io.BytesIO`, which goes through the `_tiffWriteProc` memory sink.  **Part 1: heap overflow.** `setup_env()` builds `upload.tif` (131 198 bytes) byte by byte: a mode L, 7×8191 image with `Compression=32773` (PackBits) and a 65 535-character `ImageDescription`. The sizes are picked so that when Pillow re-encodes the pixels, the strip comes to 8 + 8191 × 8 = 65 536 bytes and ends exactly at the sink's initial 64 KiB buffer. libtiff then seeks past the 126-byte IFD and writes the 65 536-byte description at offset 65 662. The sink grows only to 131 072 bytes, so the last 126 bytes of the description are written past the end of the heap block. In a fresh child process, the script runs `Image.open("upload.tif").save(<target>, "TIFF")` with no options, once with `"out.tif"` as the target and once with `io.BytesIO()`. The file save exits with 0. The BytesIO save is killed by SIGABRT, with glibc reporting `malloc(): corrupted top size`.  **Part 2: stale heap bytes in the output.** A child started with `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170` (glibc fills fresh allocations with 0x55) saves a seeded-noise 300×300 RGB image with `compression="tiff_lzw"` and four odd-length ASCII tags. It saves once to a file and once to a BytesIO, then prints every offset where the two outputs differ. libtiff skips one pad byte before the IFD and one after each odd-length tag value. The file has 0x00 at those offsets, but the BytesIO output still holds the 0x55 that was in uninitialised `realloc()` memory.  Expected output on this tree:  ``` upload.tif: 131198 bytes save to file path : exit code 0, out.tif = 131210 bytes save to BytesIO   : exit code -6, stderr: 'malloc(): corrupted top size' -> heap overflow crashed the process: True  same image, same options, saved to a file path vs. to a BytesIO:   offset 369177: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369417: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369423: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55   offset 369451: file 0x00   BytesIO 0x55  -> BytesIO output contains never-written heap bytes: True  BUG ```  The last line is `BUG` if either part shows its defect, and `OK` otherwise. With the attached patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO save exits with 0, the two outputs are identical, and the script prints `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch makes `_tiffWriteProc` in `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` honour sparse-file semantics: it sizes the buffer from the write position, and zeroes what `realloc()` adds (the initial block is already `calloc`'d, so every byte libtiff skips then reads as 0, exactly as through `TIFFFdOpen`). For the non-reallocating case (`flrealloc == 0`), where `loc > size` would also make `to_write` negative, it rejects the write with a `TIFFError`, the same idiom `_tiffReadProc` uses:  ```diff -        while (newsize < (size + state->size)) { +        while (newsize < (size + (tsize_t)state->loc)) {  … +        memset((UINT8 *)new_data + state->size, 0, newsize - state->size);          state->data = new_data;          state->size = newsize;          to_write = size; +    } else if (to_write < 0) { +        TIFFError("_tiffWriteProc", "Invalid Write at loc %" PRIu64 ", size: %" PRIu64, …); +        return 0;      } ```  `_tiffSeekProc` is left unconstrained, since libtiff legitimately seeks past the end of data; with the write proc fixed, `eof` can no longer exceed `size`, so the read-out in `ImagingLibTiffEncode` (`:1067`, `:1073`) stays within the block. With the patch applied and rebuilt, the BytesIO output is byte-identical to the file output, no AddressSanitizer report is produced for tag lengths 65410/65535/131071/196607, the code-execution chain described under Impact no longer runs its command, and the existing TIFF tests pass.  ## The patch  Size the libtiff in-memory write buffer from the write position, not its current size, and zero the space added by realloc in _tiffWriteProc  Applies to `src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c` at the commit above.  ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py index 3d804ea4a..d2a926a62 100644 --- a/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py +++ b/Tests/test_file_libtiff.py @@ -760,6 +760,38 @@ class TestFileLibTiff(LibTiffTestCase):          save_bytesio("packbits")          save_bytesio("tiff_lzw")   +    def test_save_bytesio_seek_past_end(self, tmp_path: Path) -> None: +        # When writing the directory, libtiff seeks past the end of the data +        # written so far, and then writes the tag values there. ## Summary BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.  ## Affected versions All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)  ## Root cause BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:  - delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration. - absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).  Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.  ## Reproduction Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84  Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py  A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.  ## Suggested fix Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343.  Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team (GitHub: sonicnew)  [pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30244974/pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py)

### Summary Pillow's documented PDF append path can spend disproportionate CPU time on a compact malformed PDF page tree.  An attacker who can supply an existing PDF to an application that appends an image with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` can provide a malformed `/Pages` tree where each level repeats the same child `/Pages` reference in `/Kids`. Pillow treats the graph as a tree and expands each repeated reference in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` without tracking visited or duplicate indirect references.  In the bounded proof below, a `1410`-byte PDF expands to `8192` page references from one distinct page object and takes about `9.6` seconds through the append path. A comparable linear control with the same depth stays at one page reference and completes in about `0.02` seconds.  This is in scope for Pillow's security policy because it is reproducible in `main`, affects the latest public release tested (`12.3.0`), and is not just an unexpected Python exception. The vulnerable operation accepts attacker-controlled PDF bytes through Pillow's PDF parser and causes deterministic resource consumption before normal completion.  ### Details  #### Affected versions  - Package: `Pillow` - Ecosystem: `pip` / PyPI - Affected component: `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` page-tree traversal reached from `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` PDF append handling - Runtime-tested affected release: `12.3.0` - Runtime-tested affected development version: `13.0.0.dev0` - Tested commit: `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Current source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar HEAD) = 2ccefca23d432456765be8d3c34564c65ba016b0c9da1e44ca389762f7eda054` - Release `12.3.0` commit: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Release `12.3.0` source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar 12.3.0) = 94bed33fd20123938dbc0153d295250bb4e3c09251b6d4a34f7595e25d409c81` - Source-level affected: `5.1.0`, `12.2.0`, `12.3.0`, and `HEAD` - Likely affected range: `>= 5.1.0` - Patched versions: none known  Evidence fact strings:  - Runtime-tested affected: 12.3.0 - Runtime-tested affected: 13.0.0.dev0 at b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa - Source-level affected: 5.1.0 - Source-level affected: 12.2.0 - Source-level affected: HEAD - Likely affected range: >= 5.1.0, no fixed version known - Pre-boundary note: 5.0.0 has PdfImagePlugin.py but no src/PIL/PdfParser.py  `5.0.0` contains `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` but does not contain `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`. `PdfParser.py` was introduced by `6207b44ab1ff4a91d8ddc7579619876d0bb191a4` (`2018-01-18 issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs`), which shipped in `5.1.0`.  #### Technical details  The reachable path is:  1. A service or application receives an attacker-influenced existing PDF and appends an image using Pillow's public PDF save path:     ```python    Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(existing_pdf_file, format="PDF", append=True)    ```  2. `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` routes `append=True` to `PdfParser`:     ```python    is_appending = im.encoderinfo.get("append", False)    filename_str = filename.decode() if isinstance(filename, bytes) else filename    if is_appending:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="r+b")    else:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="w+b")    ```  3. `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` parses the existing PDF and linearizes the page tree:     ```python    self.page_tree_root = self.read_indirect(self.pages_ref)    self.pages = self.linearize_page_tree(self.page_tree_root)    self.orig_pages = self.pages[:]    ```  4. `linearize_page_tree()` recursively follows every `/Kids` entry and extends the page list. It does not track page-tree node identity, duplicate references, or active traversal references:     ```python    def linearize_page_tree(        self, node: PdfDict | None = None    ) -> list[IndirectReference]:        page_node = node if node is not None else self.page_tree_root        check_format_condition(            page_node[b"Type"] == b"Pages", "/Type of page tree node is not /Pages"        )        pages = []        for kid in page_node[b"Kids"]:            kid_object = self.read_indirect(kid)            if kid_object[b"Type"] == b"Page":                pages.append(kid)            else:                pages.extend(self.linearize_page_tree(node=kid_object))        return pages    ```  5. During append, `rewrite_pages()` then iterates the expanded `orig_pages` list and scans/replaces entries in `self.pages`, adding more cost to the already expanded duplicate-reference list.  The missing invariant is:  ```text The PDF page tree should be treated as an acyclic tree of unique indirect references before Pillow builds pages/orig_pages or rewrites pages. ```  The proof intentionally uses a malformed PDF page-tree DAG: each `/Pages` node repeats the same next `/Pages` child reference twice. Pillow accepts this graph and expands it as if the repeated reference represented distinct subtrees.  ### PoC  Environment used for validation:  - OS/runtime: Linux, Python `3.13.11` - Current tested build: Pillow `13.0.0.dev0`, commit `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Latest release tested: Pillow `12.3.0` - The proof uses only synthetic in-memory PDFs and does not contact the network. Applications are impacted if untrusted users can supply an existing PDF that the application later appends to, watermarks, or exports using Pillow's `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` route. ``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk.  All three ingredients come from the file. `JpegImagePlugin` reassembles APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` chunks into `im.info["icc_profile"]` (`:238-241`) and stores the COM payload in `im.info["comment"]` (`:194`); `_save()` forwards the comment on its own — `comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment"))` (`:808`) — so the application only has to pass the ICC profile through, which is the standard way to keep colours correct when re-encoding (`docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst:608`). Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Against a long-lived stdlib-`http.server` worker running exactly the handler above (stock `/src` build, CPython 3.12 / glibc 2.36 / libjpeg62-turbo 2.1.5, ASLR/PIE/NX on, default Pillow settings, worker as root, attacker as uid 65534 given only the service address), this overflow was driven to shell command execution by the worker in two independent ways once library base addresses were known: (a) a JPEG with ~2400 APPn spray segments (heap grooming), the 65498-byte ICC profile and a 3020-byte COM whose bytes re-image the two libjpeg pools so that the real `grayscale_convert()` copies a chosen 384-byte scanline over `_PyRuntime`, setting `allocators.obj_arena.free = system` with `ctx` = the command — the request returns 200, the worker keeps serving, and the next pymalloc arena release runs the command (14/14 and 15/15 runs on fresh workers); (b) a 28-byte COM that rewrites the `size`/`next` of a groomed free tcache chunk sitting right behind the buffer so that Pillow's own `malloc(comment_size)` in the next JPEG save (`src/encode.c:1250`) returns `_imaging.so`'s writable `.got.plt`, the comment replaces `free` with `system`, and the encoder's cleanup `free(context->comment)` at `JpegEncode.c:376` runs the command (14/14, deterministic once groomed). Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. RESAVE = """ import sys from io import BytesIO from PIL import Image im = Image.open(BytesIO(sys.stdin.buffer.read())) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) print("save returned normally") """   def segment(marker, payload):     return bytes([0xFF, marker]) + struct.pack(">H", len(payload) + 2) + payload   def make_jpeg(with_comment):     """A valid 256x256 JPEG: an ICC profile of ICC_PAYLOAD bytes, optionally a COM."""     noise = random.Random(1234).randbytes(256 * 256 * 3)  # ~100 KB of image data     out = BytesIO()     Image.frombytes("RGB", (256, 256), noise).save(out, "JPEG", quality=95)     plain = out.getvalue()      icc = segment(0xE2, b"ICC_PROFILE\0\x01\x01" + b"I" * ICC_PAYLOAD)     com = segment(0xFE, COMMENT) if with_comment else b""     return plain[:2] + icc + com + plain[2:]  # splice in right after SOI   def resave(jpeg):     # -X faulthandler: on a fatal signal, print where in Python the child died     cmd = [sys.executable, "-X", "faulthandler", "-c", RESAVE]     r = subprocess.run(cmd, input=jpeg, capture_output=True)     print((r.stdout + r.stderr).decode(errors="replace").strip())     print(f"-> exit status {r.returncode}")     return r.returncode   # Control: the same file without a COM segment re-saves fine, so the buffer # sizing and the ICC profile on their own are harmless. print("Control: re-save the JPEG without a comment") resave(make_jpeg(with_comment=False))  # The bug: add a COM segment. The comment is now written into a buffer that has # no room left. print(f"\nPoC: re-save the JPEG with a {len(COMMENT)}-byte comment") rc = resave(make_jpeg(with_comment=True))  # A negative return code means the child was killed by a signal (SIGSEGV or # SIGABRT from glibc's heap checks), not by a Python exception. if rc < 0:     print(f"\nim.save() killed the process with signal {-rc}: out-of-bounds heap write")     print("BUG") else:     print("OK") ``` </details>  ---

### Summary  Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219  Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.  I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.  Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.  ### Details  ## Affected wheels  From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:  | Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status | |---|---|---| | 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** | | **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |  Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.  ## The defect  `src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:  ```c OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =     l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =     l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2; ```  `tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.  The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.  Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.  ## Patch status  Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).  The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.  ## Suggested remediation  1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file. 2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code. 3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.  ## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply  `Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.  I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.  That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.  ### Proof of concept  ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:  ``` ==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8     #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086     #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912     #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575     #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793     #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949     #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132 located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by     opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939 ```  Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.  I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.  No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.  ### Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.  **Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.  **Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):  ``` rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk ```  Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.  To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

Versions of the package pymongo before 4.6.3 are vulnerable to Out-of-bounds Read in the bson module. Using the crafted payload the attacker could force the parser to deserialize unmanaged memory. The parser tries to interpret bytes next to buffer and throws an exception with string. If the following bytes are not printable UTF-8 the parser throws an exception with a single byte.

### Summary  PyMongo passed the KMS endpoint of a data key verbatim into `parse_host()`, which returns any string ending in `.sock` unchanged instead of validating it as a hostname and port. The driver's connection code then treats such an address as a Unix domain socket path and connects to it with `AF_UNIX`. Because the endpoint originates from `masterKey.endpoint` in a key vault document, a party who can write to the key vault could redirect the driver's KMS connection to an arbitrary Unix domain socket path on the application host.  ### Impact  An application using client-side field level encryption (CSFLE) or Queryable Encryption is affected if an attacker can write to its key vault collection. Setting `masterKey.endpoint` on a data key to a `.sock`-suffixed string causes the next KMS request for that key (key cache TTL is ~60 seconds) to open an `AF_UNIX` connection to the attacker-chosen filesystem path from inside the victim application process. The documented custom KMS endpoint feature supports TCP hosts only, so this crosses a boundary the feature was never intended to allow.  Impact is limited to the side effects of the connection itself. The socket is still wrapped in a verifying TLS context using the `.sock` string as `server_hostname`, and insecure KMS TLS options are rejected, so the handshake always fails and the KMS message is never sent. The attacker controls the connect target but not the transmitted bytes (a fixed TLS ClientHello).  Applications that do not use CSFLE or Queryable Encryption are not affected. Applications whose key vault is not writable by untrusted parties are not affected.  ### Patches  Fixed in PyMongo 4.18.2 `_EncryptionIO.kms_request` now rejects a `.sock`-suffixed KMS endpoint with `pymongo.errors.ConfigurationError` immediately after parsing, before any connection is attempted, on both the synchronous and asynchronous paths. No application code changes are required beyond upgrading.  ### Workarounds  If you cannot upgrade immediately:  - Restrict write access to the key vault collection to trusted principals only. This is the recommended configuration regardless of this issue. - Validate `masterKey.endpoint` on data keys you create, and audit existing key vault documents for endpoints ending in `.sock`.  ### Details  - `_EncryptionIO.fetch_keys` reads key vault documents from the server and hands them to libmongocrypt, which surfaces the stored `masterKey.endpoint` verbatim as `kms_context.endpoint`. - `_EncryptionIO.kms_request` passed that string to `parse_host(endpoint, 443)`. `parse_host` returns entities ending in `.sock` verbatim, skipping the hostname and port validation applied to every other input. - `_create_connection` (and the async equivalent) checks `host.endswith(".sock")` and performs an `AF_UNIX` `sock.connect(host)`, treating the string as a filesystem path.

### Impact  When reading/writing via an ID with the GridFS API, require an exact match on the given ID. Otherwise, if a Hash is given in place of the ID, it may be interpreted as criteria, overriding the ID match.  ### Patches Patch available in pymongo >= 4.18.1  ### Workarounds Ensure your existing workflow _only_ supports exact matching on the GridFS API.

### Summary  PyMongo percent-decoded the entire host section of a connection string before splitting it into individual `host:port` entries. A percent-encoded `,` or `:` in a hostname therefore decoded into a real delimiter, injecting an additional attacker-chosen host and port into the client's seed list.  ### Impact  An application that interpolates untrusted input into a MongoDB connection string -- for example, a tenant name or hostname fragment taken from a request -- could be made to add an attacker-controlled server to the seed list. Because `%2C` and `%3A` survive most URL-safety checks and only become delimiters inside PyMongo's parser, input that looks like a single hostname to the application becomes two hosts to the driver. The client may then perform topology discovery and authentication against the attacker's host, exposing credentials, or route operations to it.  Unix domain socket paths, the only host identifiers that legitimately require percent-encoding, are not affected.  ### Patches  Fixed in PyMongo 4.18.2. Percent-decoding was moved into `split_hosts` and now applies only to Unix domain socket paths, identified by an unescaped `.sock` suffix before decoding, and only after splitting on `,`.  ### Workarounds  Do not interpolate untrusted input into the host portion of a connection string. If unavoidable, reject or percent-decode-and-validate the value before building the URI.  ### Details  The decoding was introduced in PyMongo 3.5.0 (PYTHON-1282), where `unquote_plus` was applied to the whole host section in `_validate_uri` and, later, `_parse_srv`, before the string was split on `,` and `:`.

An integer overflow in the BSON document encoding component of the MongoDB Python Driver's bundled native extension may occur when a single document is built from an unusually large amount of caller-supplied data. Size arithmetic is performed in a signed 32-bit type, and the guard meant to catch the overflow is written in a form whose behavior is not defined by the C language standard. A party with no privileges who can place a very large value into data that an application encodes may, depending on how the native extension was built, cause a write outside the bounds of an allocated buffer inside the application's own process.

### Impact The C extension's BSON decoder scans a Regex element's pattern and flags strings with strlen before checking the document's remaining length, so a crafted truncated Regex element can read past the end of the caller's buffer. bson.decode and bson.decode_all accept mmap and array buffers, which carry no NUL sentinel; the read can cross into unmapped memory and kill the process with an uncatchable SIGSEGV. Any application decoding untrusted BSON from such buffers is affected — impact is availability only, since the out-of-bounds bytes are never returned as content. NUL-terminated buffers (bytes, bytearray) raise `InvalidBSON` at worst; the driver's own transport and pure-Python installs are not affected. All releases through 4.18.2 are affected when the C extension is loaded.  ### Patches Fixed in PyMongo 4.18.3. Malformed Regex elements now raise InvalidBSON on every accepted buffer type; valid documents decode unchanged.  ###  Workarounds Decode untrusted BSON only from NUL-terminated buffers — bytes or bytearray — and copy mmap input first, e.g. bytes(mm[:size]).

### Summary Any project that uses Protobuf pure-Python backend to parse untrusted Protocol Buffers data containing an arbitrary number of **recursive groups**, **recursive messages** or **a series of [`SGROUP`](https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/encoding/#groups) tags** can be corrupted by exceeding the Python recursion limit.  Reporter: Alexis Challande, Trail of Bits Ecosystem Security Team [ecosystem@trailofbits.com](mailto:ecosystem@trailofbits.com)  Affected versions: This issue only affects the [pure-Python implementation](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/tree/main/python#implementation-backends) of protobuf-python backend. This is the implementation when `PROTOCOL_BUFFERS_PYTHON_IMPLEMENTATION=python` environment variable is set or the default when protobuf is used from Bazel or pure-Python PyPi wheels. CPython PyPi wheels do not use pure-Python by default.  This is a Python variant of a [previous issue affecting protobuf-java](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/security/advisories/GHSA-735f-pc8j-v9w8).  ### Severity This is a potential Denial of Service. Parsing nested protobuf data creates unbounded recursions that can be abused by an attacker.  ### Proof of Concept For reproduction details, please refer to the unit tests [decoder_test.py](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/python/google/protobuf/internal/decoder_test.py#L87-L98) and [message_test](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/python/google/protobuf/internal/message_test.py#L1436-L1478)  ### Remediation and Mitigation A mitigation is available now. Please update to the latest available versions of the following packages: * protobuf-python(4.25.8, 5.29.5, 6.31.1)

A denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability exists in google.protobuf.json_format.ParseDict() in Python, where the max_recursion_depth limit can be bypassed when parsing nested google.protobuf.Any messages.  Due to missing recursion depth accounting inside the internal Any-handling logic, an attacker can supply deeply nested Any structures that bypass the intended recursion limit, eventually exhausting Python’s recursion stack and causing a RecursionError.

sanic-cors version 2.2.0 and prior contains an improper regular expression in the try_match() function in sanic_cors/core.py that uses re.match without end-anchoring. This allows an attacker to bypass CORS origin allowlists by registering a domain that begins with a trusted origin string, to gain unauthorized access to cross-origin requests for authenticated resources.
