On Windows, `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) connect SQLite to the lock database by its path, in every directory. SQLite derives three side files from that path: `<database>-journal`, the rollback journal (pages saved to undo an interrupted write); `<database>-wal`, the write-ahead log (changes kept outside the main file); and `<database>-shm`, the shared-memory index of the WAL. SQLite acts on whichever of these it finds beside the database before the lock runs any statement. Another local account that can create files in the database's directory, but not delete files of other accounts there, places such a side file beside the database and denies everyone `DELETE` on it, which a file's creator may do. `C:\Windows\Temp` (the temporary directory of services, granting `BUILTIN\Users` create but not delete) and `C:\Users\Public` are such directories.  With a `-wal` in place, every `read_lock()` and `write_lock()` of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) raises `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error` at once, whatever `timeout` says, until that account removes its file; the lock user cannot. With a `-journal` beside a lock database that holds a table, SQLite replays the journal and deletes the file the journal names, a file of the lock user, and the acquire reports success. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the POSIX form of the defect, GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8, whose text says "Windows does not take this path" (review round 4, finding F2 of set D). The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.  The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.  Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.  ## Mechanism  Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.  A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.  ## Reproduction  The review's reproducers, quoted as received. `oplock_vm.py` section `[2]` is this finding; sections `[1a]` and `[1b]` belong to the `release()` advisory. `oplock_semantics_vm.py` is the same-account probe of which path operations wait. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.  ## Workarounds  - Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows. - Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits. - No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. `StrictSoftFileLock` and `AsyncStrictSoftFileLock` check `<path>.filelock` (the coordination directory that holds the lock's state) with one `lstat` call on its name. `lstat` reports what a name is without following a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path). After that check, the code reaches `<path>.filelock/claims` by pathname for every later operation (`mkdir`, scan, publish, link, unlink). `_open_directory` passes `O_NOFOLLOW` (a flag that makes an open fail when the final name is a symbolic link), but the flag covers only the final `claims` component. The kernel follows a symbolic link in any earlier component.  Another local user (the other user below) who can rename `<path>.filelock` exchanges it for a symbolic link after the check. In a shared directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), any user with write access can do this. Where the shared directory is sticky, such as `/tmp`, only the user who created `<path>.filelock` before the user running the lock (the lock user below) first used it can. The lock user's process (root's, if root takes the lock) then creates a `claims` directory and claim files (the files whose presence says a process wants or holds the lock) inside a directory the other user chooses but only the lock user can write.  When the link points at another strict lock's `.filelock` directory, the stranded claims make that lock time out for every process until an operator finds and force-breaks each one. The `claims` property and `force_break()` resolve the same path with no check at all. Affected versions: filelock >= 3.30.0 and <= 4.2.0 (finding `ANT-2026-SVFEYX89`).  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:H, 5.8 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:H` (high attack complexity): the swap must land between the `lstat` and the next `mkdir`. The other user does not aim at that window. It flips the name in a loop with `renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE)` (a system call that swaps two names in one step) across repeated acquires, and won after 1 to 31 runs of the lock user's program in the scanner's trials. A sticky directory also requires it to have created `<path>.filelock` first. `PR:L` (low privileges): an unprivileged account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own.  `C:L` (low confidentiality impact): through `claims`, one file name per planted link from a directory only the lock user can list. `I:L` (low integrity impact): a directory named `claims` and files with filelock's fixed claim names and contents appear, created with the lock user's privileges, in a directory the other user chooses but cannot write. The process overwrites or truncates nothing that exists. `A:H` (high availability impact): aimed at another strict lock of the lock user, the stranded claims deny that lock to every process until an operator finds and force-breaks each one. Classification from the review: security, conditional on the other user being able to rename the intermediate component. The scanner rated it high (CWE-363).  ## Scope and preconditions  - The other user can rename `<path>.filelock`. In a writable directory without the sticky bit (a `0777` or group-writable project or cache directory), any user with write permission on the directory can, even though the lock user created and owns `<path>.filelock`. In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, only the user who created `<path>.filelock` before the lock user's first use can, because that user then owns both the directory and the symbolic link (the planting precondition of GHSA-9c4x-gm8v-wgc4). - The link's target is a directory the lock user can write. The effect that matters is on that directory. An acquire that completes through the link also holds the shared lock with its claims elsewhere, but a user who can rename `<path>.filelock` can defeat that lock's exclusion anyway. - `fs.protected_symlinks=1` (a Linux setting that refuses to follow another user's symbolic link in a world-writable sticky directory) does not interfere. The link is an intermediate path component, not the last one. In the sticky-directory case it also sits in a directory the other user owns. - Missed attempts show up to the lock user as `SoftFileLockProtocolError` or `FileNotFoundError`. The swap therefore works against a lock that a program takes more than once: a periodic job, a worker pool, or a caller that retries or waits with a timeout (each poll of a waiting acquisition is a new attempt). - The two entry points that need no race (`claims` and `force_break()` on a resting symbolic link) depend on the lock user inspecting or recovering the lock. The planted link invites this by making `acquire()` fail with a protocol error. The `force_break()` variant works only when the lock user breaks claims that name a live process on its own host without checking them first, as the recovery loop in `docs/tutorials.rst` does. `docs/how-to.rst` tells the operator to verify that the named owner is gone before breaking. - Platform: POSIX, demonstrated on Linux (tmpfs and overlayfs). Windows has no `dir_fd` (file operations relative to an open directory handle), and on Windows the documented requirement is a lock directory that untrusted users cannot write.  filelock's checks against another local user hold only when no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. A user who can rename entries in a non-sticky directory above the lock controls every name below it. No file-based lock can defend against that.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit b831496, the check and the first use are adjacent lines of [`StrictSoftFileLock._acquire`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_strict.py#L123-L128). We checked both against the git tags.  ## Mechanism  On the benign path, `_ensure_protocol_directory(coordination_directory)` finds `<path>.filelock` to be a real directory, and `_ensure_protocol_directory(claim_directory)` finds `claims` inside it. The doorway (the acquire step that scans existing claims and publishes the caller's own) then publishes into it. A symbolic link resting at `<path>.filelock` stops at the first call with "is not a real directory". That answer describes the name at that instant only; nothing carries it forward. With the name exchanged for a link to a directory `T` between the two calls:  - The second call runs `mkdir("<path>.filelock/claims")`, which creates `T/claims` with the lock user's credentials. The `mkdir` succeeds, so `_ensure_protocol_directory` returns without looking at anything. - `_attempt_doorway` then works in `T/claims` for as long as the name still points there. `_read_existing_claims` uses `directory.exists()` and `os.scandir(directory)`. `_publish_record` opens the claim directory by its full path and creates `.intent-v1-<token>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp` and `intent-v1-<token>.claim` (the intent claim, which announces a pending acquire) in it. When its intent wins the scan, `_link_no_replace` adds `held-v1-<token>.claim` (the held claim, which marks the lock as taken). `_open_directory` does pass `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, but on `"<path>.filelock/claims"`, so the flag covers `claims` only. - Cleanup resolves the name again. `_unlink_in_directory` opens `<path>.filelock/claims` by path. When the name is back at the real directory by then, the `unlink` gets `ENOENT` (the "no such file" error), which `_unlink_owner_path_result` counts as removed. The claim file stays in `T/claims`.  When `T/claims` already exists, the `mkdir` takes the `FileExistsError` branch, `lstat` sees a real directory, and the same scan and publication run on the existing directory. With `T/claims` holding a file `secret-name.txt` and an old `.held-v1-<hex>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp`, the lock user's process raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError: … claim 'secret-name.txt': unknown claim name or protocol version`. `_reclaim_private_record` unlinks the private-record file. `intent-*.claim` files and a clock-probe file from `_filesystem_now` stay behind.  The window is a few lines of Python between two system calls, but the other user does not aim at it. `renameat2` with `RENAME_EXCHANGE` flips the name in a loop, so each system call of the lock user sees the directory or the link more or less at random. An attempt that sees the link at the `lstat` raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError`. One that sees the directory there and the link at the next `mkdir` is a hit. Four other ways reach the same by-name resolution. The scanner observed each of them at the same commit, with `victim` and `attacker` as separate accounts and default lock options.  The first way strands claims in another strict lock. With the swapped-in link pointing at the coordination directory of a second lock of the lock user (`/home/victim/private/db.lock.filelock`, parent mode `0700`), 200 acquires of the shared lock left 7 to 17 well-formed `intent-v1-*.claim` and `held-v1-*.claim` files in the second lock's `claims`. No process holds that lock, yet `StrictSoftFileLock("/home/victim/private/db.lock", timeout=1)` raises `Timeout` from then on, until an operator force-breaks each stranded claim.  The second way swaps one component lower, at `claims`. The claim scan does not use a descriptor (an open handle that stays bound to one directory whatever its name later points to). `os.scandir(directory)`, the record reads, `_reclaim_private_record` (called with its descriptor slot set to `None`) and the clock probe in `_filesystem_now` (`os.open(directory / name, O_CREAT | O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW)` followed by `probe.unlink()`) all go by pathname. For a sticky directory, the other user needs to have created `<path>.filelock` first. It then puts a real `claims` directory (mode `1777`) in it with one empty file named `.held-v1-<32 zeros>.claim.private-v1-<32 zeros>.tmp`, so that every scan calls the probe, and exchanges `claims` with a link in a loop.  After 200 acquires by the lock user, 14 to 42 one-byte, mode `0600`, lock-user-owned files named `.held-v1-<hex>.claim.private-v1-<hex>.tmp` are in the `0700` directory the link points to. The probe open went through the link, and the pathname `unlink` ran after `claims` was a directory again and got `ENOENT`. A swap at this level does not affect publication or release, because there `_open_directory`'s `O_NOFOLLOW` does cover `claims`.  The third way is `claims` with no race. The property calls `_read_existing_claims` on an instance that did not go through `_acquire`, and `directory.exists()` and `os.scandir(directory)` both follow a link. After the other user runs `mkdir /tmp/work.lock.filelock; ln -s /home/victim/private /tmp/work.lock.filelock/claims`, `acquire()` refuses with "is not a real directory". The inspection loop from `docs/how-to.rst` (`for claim in lock.claims: ...`) raises `SoftFileLockProtocolError: … claim 'customer-1123f274.db': unknown claim name or protocol version`. That names the first non-hidden entry, in sort order, of a directory the other user cannot list. A missing or empty target returns `()`, a non-directory gives "Not a directory" and an unreadable directory "Permission denied", so the call also tells those apart.  The fourth way is `force_break()` with no race. It confirms the name with a by-name `os.scandir` in `_require_exact_name` and unlinks through `_unlink_in_directory`, where `O_NOFOLLOW` again covers `claims` only. After the other user's one command `ln -s /home/victim/private/db.lock.filelock /tmp/service.lock.filelock`, the recovery loop from `docs/tutorials.rst` run by the lock user on `/tmp/service.lock` (`for claim in stale.claims: stale.force_break(claim.name)`) lists and removes the `held` and `intent` claims of the live holder of `/home/victim/private/db.lock`. A second process then acquires that lock while the first is still in its critical section with `is_locked == True`. The first holder's `release()` later finds its claims gone, counts `ENOENT` as removed and returns without error. Only a directory named `claims` below the link's target is reachable, so the targets are other strict locks, not arbitrary files.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-SVFEYX89`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The other user chooses the location only. filelock fixes the directory name, and the files contain filelock's own claim record (magic, token, PID, host name, start token). The process overwrites or truncates nothing that exists. This amounts to directory and file creation outside the lock's directory with the lock user's privileges, not a write of chosen data.  Where the chosen directory already has a `claims` subdirectory, the lock user's process also scans it, unlinks entries named like stale private records, and raises an error that quotes the first other file name in it. Aimed at another strict lock's `.filelock` directory, the stranded claims deny that lock to every process until an operator finds and `force_break()`s each one. Without this the other user has no way to affect a lock in a directory it cannot enter. The swap at `claims` leaves one-byte `0600` dot-files instead of claims.  Through `claims`, another user learns one file name per planted link from a directory only the lock user can list, and whether a guessed path is missing or empty, a file or a directory. This needs the exception text or its `claim_name` to reach that user (a shared log, CI output, an error report); on its own this disclosure is minor. The `force_break()` variant puts two processes inside a different strict lock's critical section, one the other user can neither list nor write, with neither told. That happens only when the lock user runs the tutorial's blind recovery loop.  This shares only the bug class with GHSA-j8f7-rjxc-mr56 (the symbolic link at the `ReadWriteLock` database path, fixed in 4.0.9). There the other user chose the file the lock opened. Here the link sits one component above the final one, the other user swaps it in after the check that refuses it, and it chooses only the parent directory.  ## Workarounds  Keep strict locks in a directory no other user can write. In a sticky shared directory, create `<path>.filelock` as the service user before any other account can, and check its owner before first use. Do not run the recovery loop from `docs/tutorials.rst` on a lock in a shared directory without first verifying, as `docs/how-to.rst` says, that the owner named in each claim is gone. Treat an unexpected `SoftFileLockProtocolError` that quotes an unknown claim name as a sign that `claims` may point elsewhere. Keep the exception text of `claims` out of logs other accounts can read. On Windows, keep the lock directory writable only by trusted users.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. Its access list, or ACL, is whatever the lock directory hands down to new files. filelock creates the `ReadWriteLock` database, which it asks to be `0o600`, the same way. In a directory whose inheritable ACL grants other local accounts access to new files, those accounts can open the lock file or database. They can take the byte-range lock (a lock on a span of bytes in a file) once the owner releases it and keep the owner's later `acquire()` calls waiting or timing out. They can read holder metadata an `on_acquired` hook left in a `preserve_lock_file=True` file. Where the directory hands down modify access, they can write to both files.  `lock.mode` still reports `0o600`. The documentation neither promises an ACL on Windows nor says that Windows drops the mode. On Unix the same mode keeps other accounts out. Mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol holds on either platform. Affected versions are filelock 3.10.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows.  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. The scanner rated this medium; the maintainers keep medium.  ## Scope and preconditions  - The affected classes are `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Windows (`WindowsFileLock`), and the SQLite database of `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock`. Both go through `_open_non_reparse_fd`. The soft locks create their markers with `os.open`, which also keeps only a read-only bit of the mode on Windows; the scanner did not examine them further. - The directory is one that other local accounts cannot write, which the documentation already requires on Windows, but whose inheritable entries grant them read (or modify) access to new files. Examples are a service's data directory readable by `Users`, or any directory with `(OI)(CI)` entries (entries that new files and sub-directories inherit) for another account. A directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts, such as one inside a user profile, hides the problem. - The other account must open the file. According to the `LockFileEx` documentation, read access is enough to take the byte-range lock, so it can hold the lock whenever the owner does not. The lock file exists while the owner holds the lock, and stays after release with `preserve_lock_file=True`. The `ReadWriteLock` database is not unlinked at any point. - Unix is not affected, because `UnixFileLock` creates the file with the mode and repeats it with `fchmod`. Mutual exclusion between cooperating processes is not affected.  ## Affected code  Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_open_non_reparse_fd` reduces the mode to one `read_only` bit](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_windows.py#L252-L253). That bit is false for every accepted mode, because [`_check_mode`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L526) rejects any mode without owner read and write, and an unset mode becomes `0o666`. The Windows backend has applied no more of the mode than that at any version, so this is a long-standing gap rather than a regression.  ## Mechanism  `_open_non_reparse_fd(path, mode)` computes `read_only = not mode & _OWNER_WRITE` and calls `_nt_open(path, read_only=read_only)`. `_nt_open` fills an `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` with the NT path and `OBJ_CASE_INSENSITIVE` and leaves `SecurityDescriptor` NULL. Per the `NtCreateFile` and `OBJECT_ATTRIBUTES` documentation, a NULL descriptor gives the new file default security, which on NTFS is the set of inheritable entries of the parent directory. A lock file created with `mode=0o600` in a directory that hands down read access to `Users` is therefore readable by `Users`.  Nothing tells the caller. In a directory that hands down read access, another account can hold the lock and make the owner wait or time out, and read holder metadata in a preserved lock file. Where the directory hands down modify access, as in the maintainers' test, it can also write the lock file and the `ReadWriteLock` database. With the mode honoured, as on Unix, a user without write access to the directory can do none of this. The exposure ends there: the effect reaches only the lock file or lock database, and mutual exclusion between processes that follow the protocol still holds.  ## Workarounds  - On Windows, keep lock files and `ReadWriteLock` databases in a directory whose ACL already excludes other accounts (inside the user profile, or a directory with inheritance disabled and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted), rather than relying on `mode`. - After creating a lock file with `preserve_lock_file=True` or a `ReadWriteLock` database, set its ACL yourself, for example `icacls <file> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:F" "SYSTEM:F" "Administrators:F"`; a file that exists keeps its ACL on later opens. - Do not store anything confidential in the lock file through `on_acquired` on Windows.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. `SoftReadWriteLock` (and `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock`, which wraps one) refreshes its holder record (the file under `<path>.rw/holders/` that says a process holds or wants the lock) on every poll of a waiting acquire and on every heartbeat (the periodic refresh a holder runs to keep its record fresh). It does so by reopening `<path>.rw/holders/<token>` by name with a plain blocking `O_WRONLY | O_NOFOLLOW` open and writing at offset 0, without checking what it opened. `O_NOFOLLOW` makes the open fail only when the final name is a symbolic link (a file that redirects to another path).  A different local user (the other user below) who owns the lock's `.rw` tree reads the token of the user running the lock (the lock user below) from the `holders/` listing and renames another node over the record. The other user owns the tree because it created it first in a sticky directory such as `/tmp` (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner rename or remove it), or because it can write a lock directory without the sticky bit.  A FIFO (a named pipe: a file whose open for writing blocks until some process opens it for reading) makes the lock user's `write_lock()` / `read_lock()` hang regardless of `timeout`. It also stops a lock holder's heartbeat thread without `on_compromise` (the callback that tells a holder it lost the lock) ever running, so the lock grants a second process while the first still believes it holds it. This works on a default Linux.  Where the kernel lets a user hard-link a file it does not own (a hard link is a second name for the same file; Linux with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`; macOS and the BSDs by their defaults, not executed), a hard link makes the lock user overwrite the first ~135 bytes of one of its own private files with its holder record. Affected versions: filelock >= 4.0.0 and <= 4.2.0. Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported it in private as `ANT-2026-AT33VEVC` [medium, CWE-62], titled "SoftReadWriteLock holder refresh writes through hard links, hangs on FIFOs".  ## Severity  **CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:H, 6.1 (Medium).**  `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `AC:L` (low attack complexity): on a default Linux there is no race. `PR:L` (low privileges): a local user with ordinary privileges is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction): the lock user's process acts on its own. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `I:L` (low integrity impact): where the kernel permits hard links to files one does not own, the lock user also writes its holder record over the first ~135 bytes of one of its private files. The bytes are filelock's record, not chosen by the other user, so the change stays within that record. `A:H` (high availability impact): the other user makes a lock user's acquire outlast any `timeout` and leaves a holder's heartbeat thread asleep. The lock then evicts the holder without telling it, and two processes believe they hold the write lock.  Classification from the external review: conditional security. The owner of a planted `.rw` tree can make the refresh open a FIFO and stall a lock user, including its heartbeat. Overwriting a file of the lock user through a hard link also needs a permissive hard-link policy. The scanner rated it medium.  ## Scope and preconditions  - Trust boundary: the other party is a different local account that owns the lock's `.rw` tree. Either it created `<path>.rw` (with `gen/` and `holders/`) before the lock's first use in a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, where `prepare()` adopts an existing tree whoever owns it and whatever its mode. Or the lock lives in a directory without the sticky bit that the account can write (the scanner checked a root-created `0777` directory). There being first is not needed, because the other user renames the lock user's own `0700` tree aside and puts its own in place; `prepare()` does not run again for a live lock object, and a waiting lock user recreates its record in the replacement. A tree the lock user already created in a sticky directory (mode `0700`) is out of reach. - FIFO variant: needs only that boundary. It works on a default Linux. `fs.protected_hardlinks` plays no part, and `fs.protected_fifos=1` (a Linux setting that refuses some opens of FIFOs in sticky world-writable directories) does not help, since it covers `O_CREAT` opens in sticky directories only, and the other user renames the FIFO into place inside its own `holders/`. - Hard-link variant: also needs a kernel that permits a hard link to a file the caller does not own. That is Linux with `fs.protected_hardlinks=0` (the kernel's built-in value; observed), while most distributions and the scanner's test image boot with `1`, under which the other user's `link()` fails with `EPERM` (operation not permitted) and the file stays untouched. macOS and the BSDs have no such restriction by default; that follows from their `link(2)` semantics, and the scanner did not execute it. The target must be a regular file the lock user may write, on the same filesystem as the lock, in a directory the other user can search. A `0600` file in a `0755` home directory qualifies; a file under a `0700` directory does not. - Platform: observed on Linux 6.1. `AsyncSoftReadWriteLock` runs the same code through an executor thread and loses that thread (from the code, not run). On Windows named pipes cannot live in a regular directory, so there is no FIFO case there. - Ancestor boundary: protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That is the case when each ancestor belongs to the lock user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.  ## Affected code  At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`, [`OsFiles.overwrite` opens by name with `O_WRONLY | O_NOFOLLOW` and writes without `fstat`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L94-L100) (`fstat` would report the type of the file behind the open descriptor), while [`read` just above it uses `O_NONBLOCK` and a regular-file check](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_storage.py#L36-L43). The code maps the heartbeat outcome at [lines 603–613](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L603-L613), and release joins the heartbeat thread for `heartbeat_interval + 1` at [line 446](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft_rw/_sync.py#L446).  ## Introduced  The unguarded reopen came with `f974328` ("fix(soft-rw): replace the state mutex with a generation log (#738)", 2026-09-17), which dropped the earlier marker code's check of the opened descriptor. It was first released in 4.0.0 (verified with `git tag --contains f974328`, which answers 4.0.0).  ## Mechanism  `OsFiles.overwrite()` refreshes a holder record by opening `holders/<token>` by name and writing at offset 0. `O_NOFOLLOW` refuses a symbolic link at that name (a planted one ends the acquire with `OSError: [Errno 40]` and the target untouched). A hard link is an ordinary directory entry, and a FIFO is not a symbolic link either. Nothing between the open and the write checks that the descriptor is the file `create()` made. Another user who can rename inside `holders/` has two ways to use the one unguarded reopen, depending on the node it puts under the lock user's record name:  1. The other user can write `holders/`. `prepare()` uses an existing protocol tree whoever owns it; it checks only the node type. In sticky `/tmp`, the user who creates `/tmp/app.lock.rw/{gen,holders}` before the lock's first use owns `holders/` and may rename over anything the lock user creates in it. In a shared directory without the sticky bit, being first is not needed. 2. The lock user publishes its record and drops the descriptor. `Participant.publish()` calls `OsFiles.create()`, which opens `holders/<token>` with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL`, writes the record and closes. The token is the file name, so the other user reads it from a listing of its own directory. 3. The other user swaps the name. Hard link: `link("/home/victim/accounts.csv", "holders/link")`, then `rename("holders/link", "holders/<token>")`; `link(2)` needs search permission on `/home/victim` and write permission on `holders/`, nothing on the file. FIFO: `mkfifo` (mode `0666`) + `rename`, so the name is absent at no point and the lock user does not take the "record is gone, recreate it" branch. 4. The lock user writes by name. Each poll of a waiting acquire (`poll_interval`, 0.25 s) runs `advance()` → `_keep_claim_fresh()` → `_refresh_nonce()` → `overwrite()`. With the hard link the lock user owns the linked file, so `O_WRONLY` succeeds and `write_all` puts `encode_holder(...)` at offset 0 without truncating. The lock user's call then ends in an ordinary `Timeout`. A granted holder does the same from its heartbeat thread every `heartbeat_interval` (30 s by default). With `heartbeat_interval=0.5`, the holder also writes through a link planted one second after it got the write lock, and `lock.compromise` stays `None`. 5. The link disappears. On `Timeout` or release, `leave()` unlinks `holders/<token>`, which is now the other user's link. The target is back to one link and `holders/` is empty.  The scanner observed this with the hard link. `victim` runs `SoftReadWriteLock("/tmp/app.lock").write_lock(timeout=2)` and waits. `attacker`, who created `/tmp/app.lock.rw` first, renames a hard link to `/home/victim/accounts.csv` (mode `0600`, owner `victim`; the `attacker` account can neither read nor write it) over the record. The same reopen with a FIFO: `open(fifo, O_WRONLY)` without `O_NONBLOCK` (the flag that makes such an open return at once) blocks until the FIFO has a reader. The scanner observed two cases on the image with its default settings.  In a waiting acquire, the code checks the deadline one level above the blocked call, so an `open` that does not return outlasts any `timeout`, and a `close()` from another thread. The lock user, with the FIFO in place of the hard link, is still inside `write_lock(timeout=2)` 12 s later, at `_storage.py:158 _attempt_open ← :143 _open ← :96 overwrite ← _protocol.py:545 _refresh_nonce ← :494 _keep_claim_fresh ← :464 advance ← _sync.py:584 _wait_for ← :512 _do_acquire_inner`; without the FIFO the same call raises `Timeout` after 2.0 s.  Inside filelock the only thing that ends the block is a peer's `read()` of the same name: its non-blocking open is a reader for a moment, the stuck open returns, and `write_all` then fails with `EPIPE` (broken pipe). Peers read a waiter's record only in `_sweep`, at most every `stale_threshold / 2` (`stale_threshold` is the age after which peers treat a record as abandoned). With a live holder on default settings `write_lock(timeout=2)` returned after 59.9 s with `BrokenPipeError` instead of `Timeout`, and with no live peer it was still blocked after 150 s. The blocked thread is also still inside `_acquire`'s `self._locks.transaction` section, so other threads acquiring through the same instance wait behind it.  For a holder's heartbeat, `heartbeat()` knows two failures. `overwrite` returning `False` is `lost`, an `OSError` is `transient`, and `_refresh` turns those into an `evicted` or a `refresh-failed` compromise. A blocked call is neither. With `heartbeat_interval=1, stale_threshold=3` and the FIFO renamed over the record after the grant: 6.5 s later `lock.compromise` is still `None`, `on_compromise` has not run, `release()` takes 2.0 s (the join timeout; 31 s with the default interval) and the `filelock-heartbeat-*` thread is still alive after it. For comparison, when someone deletes the record outright, the holder learns `evicted` at its next heartbeat.  When whoever planted the FIFO keeps it open with the pipe buffer full, the `open` succeeds and `write_all` is what blocks, and peers' reads no longer disturb it. Run that way with the same intervals, a second process read the record as `b""`, evicted the holder after `stale_threshold` and got the write lock 3.0 s later, while the first process was still in its critical section with `lock.compromise is None` and `on_compromise` not called.  ## Reproduction  The scanner's reproducer for finding `ANT-2026-AT33VEVC`, as received, ran against commit b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1. The other user makes a lock user's `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` / `read_lock` / `write_lock` hang whatever `timeout` the caller passed. That user could already keep the lock busy, in which case the lock user gets `Timeout` on time; the FIFO takes that away. Against a process that holds the lock, the FIFO stops the heartbeat thread, which is the only path by which a holder learns of its eviction. After `stale_threshold` (90 s by default) a second process takes the lock and nothing tells the first, so a live holder and its evictor both believe they hold the write lock and `on_compromise` does not run.  A user who owns the tree can already get a reader granted beside a live writer by writing one forged `gen/<N+1>` snapshot. What this bug adds is the acquire that outlasts its `timeout` and the heartbeat thread that does not return. The FIFO variant touches nothing outside the lock's own directory.  Where the kernel allows the hard link, a different local user corrupts files it has no access to, with the rights of the process that takes the lock. filelock's holder record replaces the first 135 bytes or so of the target. The other user does not choose the bytes, so the result is data destruction, not code execution: the header of a database or archive, the first lines of a configuration or credential file. This is the hard-link counterpart, on a derived name of the soft read-write lock, of the symbolic link fixes at the lock path recorded in the changelog (3.20.1 for lock file creation, 3.20.3 for `SoftFileLock`), which `O_NOFOLLOW` does not cover.  ## Workarounds  - Keep the lock path in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. - In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can, and refuse to use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account. - Keep `fs.protected_hardlinks=1` (the default on mainstream Linux distributions). `UnixFileLock`, the backend of `FileLock` and `AsyncFileLock` on Unix, empties whatever regular file it finds at the lock path once it holds the `flock` (a kernel lock on an open file). With an explicit `mode` it also chmods that file (sets its permission bits), whether or not this acquire created it. Another local user who can rename or hard-link one of the files of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the lock path gets that file truncated by the lock user's next `acquire()`. A hard link is a second name for the same file. With a mode such as `0o666` the file, still owned by the lock user, also becomes readable and writable by that other user. The other user can then read and alter everything the lock user writes to it afterwards.  `O_NOFOLLOW`, the defence added for the symlink variant (CVE-2025-68146), does not see a renamed file or a hard link. The rename route needs the file's directory to be writable without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The hard-link route into a sticky directory such as `/tmp` needs `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`, a Linux kernel setting. Affected versions are every filelock release up to and including 4.2.0 (the truncation is as old as the project; the chmod since 3.10.2).  Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private. That is the case on first use, after a reboot, after a `/tmp` cleaner, or after a release with the default `preserve_lock_file=False`, which unlinks the file. The scanner checked three ways at the scanned commit, with default kernel settings unless stated:   - rename inside a directory without the sticky bit (a group-writable project or cache directory, a root-created `0777` directory);   - rename from such a directory into a sticky one (`1777`) on the same filesystem. The sticky bit only protects entries that already exist, so the move succeeds while the lock path is free. Once the lock user's lock file exists there, the same move fails with `EPERM`;   - `link(2)` into a sticky directory. This needs a system that lets a user hard-link a file it cannot write, which on Linux means `fs.protected_hardlinks=0`. Mainstream distributions set 1, which refuses the link. The scanner did not test macOS or the BSDs. - What the lock user loses: with the default `FileLock(path)` the lock truncates the file, which keeps its mode. With an explicit permissive `mode`, the other user can read and modify everything the lock user writes afterwards, while the file still belongs to the lock user. The other user can rename the file back to its old name after the acquire. It stays there with the lock's mode, and the lock user's next acquire creates a fresh lock file.  Somebody who may rename a single-name file may also unlink it, so losing such a file under its name is not new. What the lock adds are two operations on the inode that the other user cannot perform, `ftruncate` and `fchmod`, run with the lock user's privileges. The other user does not choose the mode, and the lock user writes no bytes the other user chose. The code parses the content into `pid`, `hostname` and start token and hands them to `owner_is_stale`, whose docstring promises to return `True` "only when this process can prove the exact recorded owner is dead". That proof holds only if the owner wrote the record. A process of another account that can open the marker for writing uses `O_WRONLY | O_TRUNC` (no `O_CREAT`, so `fs.protected_regular` does not block it) and writes `2147483647
<host>
`, keeping the host line. The host matches, PID 2147483647 does not exist, and `owner_is_stale` returns `True`.  `break_lock_file` renames the marker to `<lock>.break.<pid>.<token>` and unlinks it. Its mtime and inode guard compares against what the contender read after the rewrite, so it passes. The contender, which runs as the marker's owner, does the rename, so the sticky bit allows it. On the next poll the contender's `O_EXCL` create succeeds. The first holder is not told: `SoftFileLock` has no heartbeat, and on release `_unlink_open_marker` finds another inode or no file at the path and returns without an error.  Other records lead to the same break, each run by the scanner the same way: the holder's own PID and host with a different third line (`owner_is_stale` reads a live PID with another start token as a recycled PID); an empty file (malformed, broken after `MALFORMED_LOCK_AGE_THRESHOLD`, 2 s). `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` apply `owner_is_stale` to the `pid=`, `host=` and `start=` fields of a protocol 2 record, and rewriting `pid=` admitted a second process for both. A `SoftFileLease` holder learns of it at its next heartbeat through `on_compromise`; `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` holders do not learn of it at all.  The marker becomes writable by another account in two ways. An explicit `mode` with group or other write bits goes through `fchmod`, so the umask does not narrow it (`test_lock_mode_soft` at the scanned commit pins `-rw-rw-rw-` under umask `022`). The default mode passes `0o666` to `os.open`, so under umask `002` the marker is `0o664`. With no `mode` argument, in a setgid and sticky group directory (`3770`), a second member of the group rewrote the marker and a second process of the holder's user acquired the same way. Under umask `000` the marker is `0o666` and any local user can rewrite it. `FileLock(mode=0o666)` on a filesystem where `flock` fails with `ENOSYS` falls back to `SoftFileLock` and produces the same `-rw-rw-rw-` marker (confirmed with `fcntl.flock` replaced by a stub raising `ENOSYS`). With no `lifetime` set, `SoftFileLock` and `MarkerSoftFileLock` give neither process a signal. Whatever the lock protects (a cache, an install directory, a state file) then has two concurrent writers. The other user chooses the moment and gains nothing else: it touches no file other than the marker. The process that rewrites the record runs under a different UID from the holder; the same-UID contender only follows the protocol.  ## Workarounds  Do not give soft markers group or other write bits: pass no `mode` (or `mode=0o644`) under umask `022`. The write bits matter only for the native `flock` lock and for `FileLock`'s first open before it falls back to a soft lock. Avoid umask `002` or `000` for processes that take soft locks in directories shared with other accounts, and keep lock files in a directory other users cannot write.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. `ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) run `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY` on a fresh connection for every acquire. That statement makes SQLite load the whole schema (the `sqlite_master` table, which lists every table and index with its `CREATE` text) of whatever file sits at the lock path. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout`, which bounds waits for another connection's lock, not schema loading. The only content checks reject non-regular files and WAL mode (write-ahead log, an SQLite mode that keeps changes in a side file). A local user who can place or overwrite the file at a `ReadWriteLock`'s database path can therefore make every `acquire_read` / `acquire_write` of every process using that lock ignore its `timeout` and `blocking=False`. That position needs a non-sticky shared directory, or a database owned by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) that other users may write.  One 37 KB crafted file stalls each acquire for as long as its author chooses while the process allocates about 1 GB. A second 28 KB layout makes the acquire of a free lock run without end, spinning at 100% CPU and ignoring Ctrl-C. The effect is availability only: the other user reads nothing and corrupts nothing. Affected versions are filelock 3.20.4 through 4.2.0. One way: the lock directory is writable by that account and not sticky (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it), for example a group-writable project or cache directory. The other way: the lock user's own database is writable by that account (`0666`), which is the setup a lock shared between accounts needs. In a `1777` directory the scanner wrote the crafted file over such a database in place, and the lock user's next acquire hung. The lock user must be able to open the file read-write, so a file the other user creates is `0666`. - Sticky directories and kernel settings. In a sticky world-writable directory such as `/tmp`, Linux with `fs.protected_regular=2` (a kernel setting) refuses the lock user's `O_CREAT` open of a file owned by the other account with `EACCES`. A database owned by the other user does not work there. That does not cover a `0666` database owned by the lock user. The scanner did not test systems with `fs.protected_regular=0` (the kernel's own default). - Platform. Every platform runs the same statements. On Windows the documentation already requires a lock directory that untrusted users cannot write, so the shared-directory setup is outside what the project supports there. - Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. The caller's `timeout` reaches SQLite only as `busy_timeout` (lines 814 to 816 and 823 to 826), which limits how long SQLite waits for another connection's file lock. Loading the schema is not a wait, so nothing limits it. `blocking=False` and `timeout=0` reach SQLite as `busy_timeout=0` and stall the same way (2.4 s each with a 5-row file). `acquire_write` runs the same pragma. `AsyncReadWriteLock.read_lock(timeout=1)` stalls the same way (4.7 s with 10 rows; wrapping the acquire in `asyncio.wait_for(..., 2)` does not return earlier). A second `acquire_read` on the same instance stalls for as long as the first.  The constructor is not affected. Its validation connection (lines 484 and 485) runs no statement, so the lock user sees nothing until the first acquire. A stack dump taken 2 s into the stall shows the thread in `_configure_and_begin` at the `executescript` call. The lock accepts any SQLite file that is a regular file and not in WAL mode, whoever created it. The file does not store the text. Each row's cell names page 2 as its first overflow page (a page that holds the part of a row too large for its own page), and the "next overflow page" field of page 2 names page 2 again. SQLite builds each row from the same 4 KB page, read about 244,000 times over. The header claims 244,142 pages, because SQLite rejects a record larger than page size times page count. The script extends the file to that length as a hole (unallocated space that reads as zeros), because SQLite also rejects a file shorter than its header claims. Eight rows fit in one 4 KB leaf page. The statements are valid `CREATE TABLE`s, so SQLite reports no error, and after the stall the acquire succeeds; it does not raise `Timeout`. In a 28,672-byte file of seven 4 KB pages, pages 1 to 6 are `sqlite_master` interior pages whose 660 cell pointers all name one 5-byte cell. The lock creates its database `0600`, and leaving it that way keeps other accounts from supplying its content. The stale-lock break shared by `SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock` and `SoftFileLease` (and their async variants, and a `FileLock` that has fallen back to a soft lock on `ENOSYS`, the "not implemented" error) recognises the marker it judged stale by two values. The marker is the lock file at `<path>`, whose presence says a process holds the lock. The values are its inode number (the kernel's identity for a file, independent of its name) and its modification time (mtime) not being newer. The check runs after the contender has already closed the marker, so nothing keeps the inode allocated.  On a filesystem that hands a freed inode number straight to the next file (ext4, xfs, overlayfs on them) the next holder's marker can carry that number. A contender still between its read and its break then renames and unlinks the live marker. Another local user (the other user below) who can create files in the lock's directory, a sticky `/tmp` included (the sticky bit is a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove it), forces this at will. It plants a marker with a stale owner record and a modification time in the future and unlinks it as soon as a contender has read it. Two processes of the user running the lock (the lock user below) then hold the same default-configured lock at once, and nothing raises or logs. The original holder does not notice. `is_locked` is its own counter, and `_release` removes its claims by name through `_unlink_owner_path_result`, which takes `FileNotFoundError` as "already removed". The right to do it comes from filelock's `mkdir`, not from anything the application asked for. In the same setting the other user can neither read nor remove the `0600` sentinel in the sticky parent. With the common umask `022` and no default ACL the directories are `0755`. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share a `SoftReadWriteLock` between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory. - In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, make sure the locking account creates `<path>.rw` before anyone else can (for example at install time with mode `0700`), and do not use a lock path whose `<path>.rw` belongs to another account. - Prefer a fresh lock object per unit of work over a long-lived singleton when other accounts can write the lock directory. A fresh object re-runs the directory check and refuses a planted tree.  ## Patched version  4.2.1. ### Summary  A path traversal vulnerability in `PackageIndex` was fixed in setuptools version 78.1.1  ### Details ```     def _download_url(self, url, tmpdir):         # Determine download filename         #         name, _fragment = egg_info_for_url(url)         if name:             while '..' in name:                 name = name.replace('..', '.').replace('\\', '_')         else:             name = "__downloaded__"  # default if URL has no path contents          if name.endswith('.[egg.zip](http://egg.zip/)'):             name = name[:-4]  # strip the extra .zip before download   -->       filename = os.path.join(tmpdir, name) ```  Here: https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/blob/6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558/setuptools/package_index.py#L810C1-L825C88  `os.path.join()` discards the first argument `tmpdir` if the second begins with a slash or drive letter. `name` is derived from a URL without sufficient sanitization. While there is some attempt to sanitize by replacing instances of '..' with '.', it is insufficient.  ### Risk Assessment As easy_install and package_index are deprecated, the exploitation surface is reduced. However, it seems this could be exploited in a similar fashion like https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r9hx-vwmv-q579, and as described by POC 4 in https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-cx63-2mw6-8hw5 report: via malicious URLs present on the pages of a package index.  ### Impact An attacker would be allowed to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem with the permissions of the process running the Python code, which could escalate to RCE depending on the context.  ### References https://huntr.com/bounties/d6362117-ad57-4e83-951f-b8141c6e7ca5 https://github.com/pypa/setuptools/issues/4946

setuptools is a package that allows users to download, build, install, upgrade, and uninstall Python packages. A path traversal vulnerability in `PackageIndex` is present in setuptools prior to version 78.1.1. An attacker would be allowed to write files to arbitrary locations on the filesystem with the permissions of the process running the Python code, which could escalate to remote code execution depending on the context. Version 78.1.1 fixes the issue.

setuptools is a package that allows users to download, build, install, upgrade, and uninstall Python packages. Prior to 83.0.0, FileList applied MANIFEST.in exclude, global-exclude, recursive-exclude, and prune directives by matching compiled glob patterns against on-disk file names without Unicode normalization, so on macOS APFS or HFS+ an NFD file name could bypass an NFC exclusion rule and be packed into a source distribution. This issue is fixed in version 83.0.0.

## Summary  When building a source distribution (`python -m build --sdist` / `setup.py sdist`), setuptools' `FileList` applies `MANIFEST.in` directives (`exclude`, `global-exclude`, `recursive-exclude`, `prune`) by matching a compiled glob against on-disk file names **byte-for-byte, with no Unicode normalization**. On normalization-preserving filesystems (notably macOS APFS and HFS+), a file written in NFD and a `MANIFEST.in` rule written in NFC refer to the same file but are byte-distinct, so the exclusion silently fails to match. A file the maintainer intended to exclude is then packed into the `.tar.gz` and, if published, uploaded to the public, immutable PyPI index.  ## Details  File names in `FileList.files` come from `os.walk` (`setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`, `_find_all_simple`), so on APFS a file written NFD is offered to the matcher in NFD, while the `MANIFEST.in` pattern carries the author's editor form (typically NFC). The matching path performs no canonicalization:  ```python # setuptools/command/egg_info.py  (FileList.global_exclude) def global_exclude(self, pattern):     match = translate_pattern(os.path.join('**', pattern))   # fnmatch.translate -> regex, no NFC/NFD     return self._remove_files(match.match)                   # byte-level regex over raw os.walk names ```  A rule written NFC (`café` = `63 61 66 c3 a9`) does not match an on-disk name written NFD (`café` = `63 61 66 65 cc 81`), even though the filesystem treats the two as one file.  A `unicodedata.normalize('NFD', ...)` helper exists in `setuptools/unicode_utils.py` (`decompose()`), but it is **never called in the manifest matching path**, so neither the pattern nor the walked path is normalized before matching. The only normalization in this area, `EggInfoCommand._manifest_normalize`, uses `filesys_decode` (bytes→str decode only, no NFC/NFD) and runs when writing `SOURCES.txt`, after matching has already occurred.  ## Impact  `MANIFEST.in` exclusions are the documented mechanism maintainers use to keep secrets, local configs, and private fixtures out of the published sdist. A non-ASCII excluded file may be published to the public, immutable PyPI index despite the rule — an irreversible disclosure with no visual cue (NFC and NFD forms render identically). Exposure is filesystem-dependent and most relevant on macOS APFS/HFS+, where many maintainers build and publish. Pure-ASCII rules are unaffected.  ## Proof of concept  With a project containing `MANIFEST.in`:  ``` global-include *.txt *.json global-exclude secret_café.txt    # rule saved NFC ```  and an on-disk file `secret_café.txt` written in NFD, `python -m build --sdist` packs the secret file into the resulting `.tar.gz`, while an ASCII control file excluded by the same directive is correctly dropped — isolating the bypass to the NFC-pattern vs. NFD-name mismatch. Reproduced on macOS APFS with setuptools 82.0.1.  ## Remediation  Normalize both the walked path and each `MANIFEST.in` pattern to a single canonical form before matching, in both `setuptools/command/egg_info.py` (`FileList`) and the vendored `setuptools/_distutils/filelist.py`. For an exclusion list, err toward excluding more, and document that `MANIFEST.in` matching is normalization-insensitive on macOS.  ## Credit  Reported by Tomas Illuminati. Coordinated via CERT/CC VINCE VU#604762.

### Summary  On Windows, attacker-controlled content in a wheel's `.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt` can cause setuptools' legacy wheel installation path to create an `__init__.py` outside the requested `destination_eggdir`.  The attacker can influence the destination path, but not the contents of the created file.  ### Details  Tested setuptools commit:  `6ead555c5fb29bc57fe6105b1bffc163f56fd558`  Relevant source:  `setuptools/wheel.py`  SHA-256:  `359b7e0d5dd8c3135653abe08a8ed5dc0352eadfd7df22cb5e2b5303b7c3cafd`  The relevant call path is:  `Wheel(wheel_path).install_as_egg(destination)` → `_install_as_egg` → `_convert_metadata` → `_fix_namespace_packages`  A wheel can provide attacker-controlled content in:  `<distribution>.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  The namespace value is eventually used approximately as:  ```python mod_dir = os.path.join(destination_eggdir, *mod.split('.')) mod_init = os.path.join(mod_dir, '__init__.py')  If mod is a Windows drive-qualified absolute path containing no dots, mod.split('.') preserves it as a single component. On Windows, os.path.join(destination_eggdir, absolute_component) discards the original base directory and resolves to the attacker-supplied absolute path. The existing wheel filename and ZIP traversal checks do not validate this metadata value before it is subsequently interpreted as a filesystem path.  ```markdown ### PoC  The reproduction was performed entirely inside a disposable temporary directory.  Layout:  ```text sandbox/     destination/     outside/     input/     canary.txt ```  A synthetic wheel was created containing:  `demo_pkg-1.0.dist-info/namespace_packages.txt`  whose content was the absolute path of:  `sandbox\outside`  The real acquired setuptools implementation was then invoked:  ```python setuptools.wheel.Wheel(synthetic_wheel).install_as_egg(     sandbox_destination ) ```  The operation completed without exception.  Expected metadata was created under:  `sandbox\destination\EGG-INFO`  but setuptools also created:  `sandbox\outside\__init__.py`  The file did not exist before execution.  Its contents were:  ```python __import__('pkg_resources').declare_namespace(__name__) ```  The unrelated canary remained byte-identical.  The sandbox was deleted after recording the evidence. ```   ### Impact  A crafted wheel can cause setuptools to create a fixed-content `__init__.py` outside the intended installation directory at a filesystem path influenced by the wheel, with the permissions of the process performing the installation.  The demonstrated reproduction required the target parent directory to already exist.
